title: Iran Fired Missiles Over Residential Kuwait Again. India Has 52,000 Reasons to Worry.
excerpt: Seven ballistic missiles targeted Kuwait and Bahrain on Saturday. More than 52,000 Indians have already been evacuated from the Gulf since March. The flights keep getting cancelled.
body:
Iran launched seven ballistic missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain early Saturday morning, the second major attack on Gulf states in a week. Sirens sounded across Bahrain. Kuwait's air defences engaged all seven missiles over residential areas. No casualties were reported this time — but the last attack on Kuwait's airport killed an Indian national and injured more than sixty.

The latest salvo came after the United States struck Iranian coastal radar installations on Qeshm Island and at Goruk in the Strait of Hormuz, responding to four Iranian drones that U.S. Central Command said were threatening maritime traffic. Iran's Revolutionary Guards called the American strikes a violation of the April 8 ceasefire and fired back.

For the nine million Indians who live and work across the Gulf, Saturday's escalation was not a geopolitical abstraction. It was another day of checking whether flights were still running.

## Flights Grounded, Corridors Shrinking

On June 7, at least fifteen flights were suspended from Kuwait International Airport. IndiGo, FlyDubai, Gulf Air, Oman Air, Qatar Airways, Emirates, Etihad, and Royal Jordanian all pulled services. Routes connecting Kuwait to India, the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, and Europe were disrupted.

Kuwait's airport had only partially reopened after the previous week's attack damaged a passenger terminal. The terminal where an Indian worker died — struck by debris during an Iranian missile barrage — remains under repair.

Since the war began on February 28, India has evacuated more than 52,000 nationals from the Gulf region. Another 1,200 were pulled out of Iran itself through overland routes via Armenia and Azerbaijan, according to the Ministry of External Affairs. The MEA's Special Control Room remains operational around the clock.

## Peace Talks Have Stalled

The three-month war between the United States and Iran has settled into a grim pattern: fragile ceasefires, periodic skirmishes, and no breakthrough.

Iran wants access to $24 billion in frozen assets, sanctions waivers on crude exports, and the lifting of the American blockade on its ports. The United States wants Iran to stop threatening maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed.

On Saturday, Pakistan stepped in as a mediator. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi flew to Tehran carrying what he described as a special letter from Pakistan's army chief and prime minister to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Whether the letter moves the needle remains to be seen.

Mohsen Rezaei, an adviser to Khamenei, told CNN on Friday that talks are at a deadlock and hinge entirely on the asset release. The U.S. response was to escalate in the opposite direction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has now directed his team to assess whether Iranian assets can be redirected to Gulf states to pay for rebuilding — not just future damage, but retroactive repairs.

President Trump, facing mounting domestic pressure over rising gas prices, told NBC that Iran retains roughly 21 to 22 percent of its pre-war missile capability.

## India's Oil Lifeline Is Being Rerouted

The Hormuz blockade has forced India to structurally reshape its energy sourcing. Indian refiners have increased crude purchases from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria to cover shortfalls from the Middle East.

Venezuela is now on track to become India's fourth-largest oil supplier — a position it never held before the war. Russia's share of India's oil imports hit an eleven-month high of 38 percent in April, with India paying a 425 percent premium over its March rate for Russian crude.

OPEC+ is expected to agree on Sunday to a fourth consecutive monthly increase in output targets, but the war is preventing several member states from actually pumping more. The oil that India needs is available — it just costs more and travels farther.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The Gulf is home to the largest concentration of Indians anywhere outside India. More than 3.4 million live in the UAE alone. Another 1 million are in Kuwait, 2.6 million in Saudi Arabia, and nearly 700,000 in Bahrain, Qatar, and Oman combined.

Every missile that crosses Kuwaiti airspace crosses over their neighbourhoods. Every flight cancellation strands workers trying to visit families back home. Every airport closure delays the remittances — worth over $32 billion annually from the Gulf — that support households across Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Rajasthan.

India's embassies across the region continue to operate 24/7 helplines. The government has urged all Indian nationals to follow local authority guidelines and monitor embassy advisories. But as the war drags into its fourth month with no deal in sight, the question is no longer whether India can evacuate its citizens. It is whether they should still be there at all.
